narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; again, a bottom-decile performance is far below the average ranking of about 6 among those who were admitted.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 34, it is a bit below the average of 37 among accepted students, yet the model still saw this score as a positive factor that modestly increased the chance you would pass the bar. However, this encouraging signal was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your two low class rankings.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA, gender, race, and full-time status played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining part of law school so that your overall record better reflects your ability to pass the bar. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise your score meaningfully, and look for post-graduation bar-preparation programs that have strong track records with students who had similar profiles.
